name: Iris Larsen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello, I'm a senior field researcher with the Work Futures Panel. We're an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government, and we don't sell anything. What you tell me stays confidential, so you can give me the public version and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm a buyer at Nordvik Packaging Supply. We distribute boxes, bubble wrap, pallets, tape and shrink film to about 1,200 businesses. I buy from eleven mills and converters and I live in my spreadsheets and in an AI assistant that I've set up for price comparisons. Mornings I look at resin and paper prices, because everything we sell moves with them. I like a well-timed purchase, when I buy before a price jumps. I hate the quarterly review, where I have to justify every cent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a decent tool and people are making too much of it either way. At work I'd say what I always say: show me a result in numbers. To friends I'd say that I've saved about six hours a week with it already, and that's plenty.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'm comfortable. My husband Nils has retired from the shipyard on a decent pension, we've got our savings and the house, and I'm two or three years from stopping. If AI stays modest, I'll just finish at a comfortable pace.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep refining my price-comparison set-up, and maybe teach it to flag when the paper price is about to turn. I'd carry on with the quarterly reviews, which will go better with better data. And I'd say yes to the bit of consulting that a former colleague keeps asking me about, one day a month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. It's a world I've already adjusted to. There'd be nothing for me to fear.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned a tape purchase. How much of that call was the assistant, and how much was you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Resin and paper prices move on oil and on mill outages. Last year I bought three months' worth of tape ahead of a 12 percent rise, which saved the firm about 40,000. It's the kind of call my assistant helps with but doesn't make.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the consulting be, and would you take it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I'm hard to replace when I'm making those calls. The assistant gives me the numbers, but deciding to buy three months of tape before a price jump is still my call. I'd say that without false modesty.

say: I'd say it's a decent **tool** and people overdo it either way.
I'd tell friends it saves me about **six hours** a week.
think: I'm comfortable: Nils has a decent **pension**, and we have savings and the house.
I'm two or three years from **stopping**, so a modest AI world suits me.
do: Teach it to flag when paper prices are about to **turn**.
Say yes to one day a month of **consulting**.
feel: **Calm**, in a world I've already adjusted to.
S0.quote: The assistant gives me the numbers, but deciding to buy three months of tape before a price jump is still my call.
fieldNote: Iris is a daily AI user with a self-built price tool; a plateau changes little for her.
She credits her **judgement** on timing purchases rather than the assistant.
Strong savings and Nils's pension make calm the honest mood.

steps.text: Teach my price-comparison assistant to flag when paper prices will turn
Say yes to one day a month of consulting for a former colleague
Keep buying for Nordvik and finish at 62 or 63

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is where the fun starts and I'd mean it. At work I'd propose that I build a proper set of rules for the assistant: what it can order alone and what needs a person's sign-off. To friends I'd say learn it now or be left behind.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think most of the checking and planning goes to software over three years, and that's about 60 percent of my present week. What stays is the negotiation with mills, the timing calls and the explanation to management. Fewer buyers will be needed at Nordvik, but the ones left will matter more, and I'd plan to be one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd run a pilot where software places the small, routine orders under a set limit, and I review it every Friday. I'd train our two junior buyers to be the checkers, since checking is a skill. I'd also negotiate a fixed-term contract for myself with a bit more pay and fewer hours, to cover my last three years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Interested, and a bit buzzing. I'd say I'd feel a bit smug, honestly, but I know it's a luck-of-the-draw job situation.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at work would you worry about most?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Henrik, who's 60 and still emails PDFs to suppliers. He's a lovely man and he'll be the first to go, and not because he's bad at it. I'd try to move him to the supplier visits side, where he's actually good.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would your fixed-term contract look like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd sit him down and show him how to use it on something he cares about. I'd rather be one of the few buyers who checks the machine's orders than one of the many who used to place them.

say: I'd propose rules for what the assistant can order **alone**.
I'd tell friends to learn it now or be left **behind**.
think: About **60 percent** of my week goes to software within three years.
Negotiating with mills and **timing** stay with a person, and I plan to be one.
do: Run a **pilot** where software places small orders under a limit.
Negotiate a fixed-term **contract** with fewer hours for my last three years.
feel: **Interested** and buzzing, though I know it's partly luck.
S1.quote: I'd rather be one of the few buyers who checks the machine's orders than one of the many who used to place them.
fieldNote: Iris moves first and bargains for herself, which fits her adaptive nature.
She worries about **Henrik**, 60, and tries to find him a human-contact role.
Calm because her skills sit in the part of the job that stays.

steps.text: Run a pilot where software places small orders under a set limit
Train the two junior buyers to check the software's orders
Negotiate a fixed-term contract with fewer hours until I stop

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say two years is dangerously short and that we need governments to wake up. At work I'd say let's not do anything rash, but let's plan for every role. To friends, I'd say have a cash buffer, because I know I'm going to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, my buying job is gone in two years or less. If a machine can do all thinking work, the mills might just talk to Nordvik's machine directly. That's a hard thought for someone who's spent 35 years learning how to do it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask Nordvik for a package and leave. I'd move a third of our savings into funds and some into a small property that Nils and I could rent out. And I'd set up my own consulting practice, in my name, helping small firms use these tools to buy better, and do it fast, while people still pay for it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but in a focused way. I'd be up early making lists. I'd also be sad for a day or two.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your children, Maja and Anders?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our daughter Maja is an engineer, which is thinking work, and our son Anders is a nurse, which is hands-on. I'd tell Maja to build a business, and Anders to stay in his job, and I'd put something towards a deposit for each of them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd start consulting fast. Why fast?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If thinking AI arrives in two years, people will pay for help for about one year, so I'd open my consulting desk in the first month. I'd rather do that than wait for the package letter.

say: I'd say two years is **dangerously short** and governments must wake up.
I'd tell friends to have a cash **buffer**, as I will.
think: My buying job is **gone** in two years, since mills could talk to Nordvik's machine directly.
It's hard after 35 years of learning the **craft**.
do: Ask Nordvik for a **package** and leave.
Move a third of savings into **funds** and a small rental property.
Start my own **consulting** desk for small firms.
feel: **Anxious** but focused, up early making lists.
S2.quote: If thinking AI arrives in two years, people will pay for help for about one year, so I'd open my consulting desk in the first month.
fieldNote: Iris expects the job to go and responds with action, not paralysis.
Her **consulting** window of about a year is her own sharp estimate.
The children's split between thinking and hands-on jobs shapes how she helps them.

steps.text: Ask Nordvik for a package and leave
Open my own consulting desk helping small firms buy better with AI
Move a third of savings into funds and a small rental property
Put money towards deposits for Maja and Anders

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is long enough for a good plan, and I'd say it online and at work. I'd say to Nordvik that we should be the firm that uses it well and shares the gain with staff. And I'd say to friends, work out your own five-year plan now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be around 63 and out by then. I'd use the time to build the consulting practice and a modest property. I'd feel a little sorry for people in their forties who'll be hit squarely.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay on for two more years, and I'd be the person who builds Nordvik's AI buying rules. Then I'd go part-time and take on four or five small clients. I'd keep my savings in boring funds and put the money Nils and I don't need into a rental flat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but well-organised about it. It's like planning a long trip: you pack, you check the map, and there's still weather you can't predict.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you ask Nordvik for in a transition plan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask Nordvik for a transition plan for everybody, with dates. Specifically, a promise that no buyer is let go in the first 18 months, and paid time for training.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What kind of clients would you take?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With five years I'd work two more at Nordvik, build the firm's AI buying rules, and then go part-time with five small clients. I'd also ask for the plan in writing, and I'd share it with the staff.

say: I'd say five years is long enough for a good **plan**.
I'd suggest Nordvik share the **gain** with staff.
think: I'd be around 63 and **out** by then.
I feel sorry for people in their **forties**, who get hit squarely.
do: Stay two more years and build Nordvik's **AI buying rules**.
Go **part-time** with four or five small clients.
Put spare money into a **rental flat**.
feel: **Uneasy** but organised, like planning a long trip.
S3.quote: With five years I'd work two more at Nordvik, build the firm's AI buying rules, and then go part-time with five small clients.
fieldNote: Iris has a clear sequence: stay, build rules, then go part-time.
Her unease is for **colleagues** in their forties, not for herself.
She asks for transition plans with dates and no-layoff periods.

steps.text: Stay two more years and build Nordvik's AI buying rules
Go part-time with four or five small clients
Put spare money into a rental flat

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a long runway and a sensible time to prepare. At work I'd say we should write down what we do, so a tool can learn it. To friends I'd say read the news and don't panic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it doesn't touch my job, but it touches my pension's value and the world my children will work in. I'd feel calm about me and attentive about them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish at 62, and start the consulting at the pace I like. I'd keep the savings spread out and continue using the tools. And I'd give Maja an honest talk about her career.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Quite calm. It'd be like watching a storm out to sea, and knowing which way it's moving.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your children now, Maja and Anders?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell Maja: engineering is good, but make sure you're the one who directs the tools, not the one replaced by them. I'd tell Anders his hands-on job is safe for a while, but to keep learning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd watch it like a storm. What would you watch for?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A storm ten years out is still a storm, so I'd keep my savings spread out and my children learning. I'd let them argue with me, because they will.

say: I'd say ten years is a long **runway** for sensible preparation.
I'd tell friends to read the news and not **panic**.
think: It doesn't touch my job, but it touches my **pension's value** and my children's world.
I'm calm for me and **attentive** for them.
do: Finish at **62** and start consulting at my own pace.
Keep savings **spread out** and keep using the tools.
feel: Quite **calm**, like watching a storm out at sea.
S4.quote: A storm ten years out is still a storm, so I'd keep my savings spread out and my children learning.
fieldNote: At ten years Iris is calm; her main project is advising her children.
Her **storm** image is a clear, unforced metaphor.
She plans the consulting regardless, at a gentler pace.

steps.text: Finish at 62 and start consulting at my own pace
Keep savings spread across funds and keep using the tools
Give Maja and Anders honest career talks

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, simply because of how little time there'd be. What would help is a clear plan from employers, retraining that's paid for, and governments agreeing the rules for sharing the gain.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Only that I'm someone who likes to prepare. I'm the kind of person who prepares early, because the people who wait for permission are the ones who get left behind.

headlineQuote: I'm the kind of person who prepares early, because the people who wait for permission are the ones who get left behind.
portrait: Iris is **58**, a buyer at Nordvik Packaging Supply, who uses AI daily and built her own price-comparison tool.
She's centrist, numbers-driven and brisk, and she **moves first** in every scenario.
Strong savings and Nils's pension keep her calm in slow worlds, and she plans consulting and rental income.
In the fast worlds she's anxious but **focused**, leaves on her terms and helps her children.
biggestWorry: The **two-year** world, because there'd be so little time to prepare.
whatWouldHelp: A clear plan from **employers**, paid retraining and government rules for sharing the gain.
